1815133729750503771 [2024-07-21] @algekalipso 💜 60 🔁 2
On the one hand, a lot of peak positive valence experiences are described as being very simple in their features.

Look at the formless jhanas where you, in a manner of speaking, become pure space or purify your awareness. You experience awareness devoid of content, allegedly, or even an all-pervasive sense of utter nothingness and beyond. These empirically are very healing and psychologically beneficial, as well as proximal to a sense of well-being.

On the other hand, we have the very broad, straightforward intuition that we enjoy diverse experiences.

How do we reconcile these two points?

In the past, at Qualia Research, we have developed a lot of frameworks that seem to reconcile these facts.

For example, we postulate the existence of a sort of boredom mechanism: when the system recognizes that you are not learning over a period of time, it adds dissonant vibrations to your experience at a subtle level that makes you feel uncomfortable and irritable, which itself is a higher complexity state of consciousness with asymmetries, which Johnson's Symmetry Theory of Valence (2015) would indicate are unpleasant, at least if we use the frame I developed of consonance, dissonance, and noise signatures (2017).

More so, we are built in such a way that novelty energizes our system, and then this energization has downstream effects such as neural annealing, which smooths out the field of awareness and increases your overall valence. The prototypical example of this is when you eat very hot peppers, which are very unpleasant in the mouth, but trigger waves of euphoria in the body, which themselves are very simple and harmonious.

However, this time I am going to elaborate on another way of reconciling these intuitions and observations.

Hedonium, or matter optimized for pure well-being, is usually depicted as an extremely simple experience of, let's say, pure love. But if you look at the gradient of extremely amazing experiences, many of them are in fact combining a lot of different qualia varieties and gestalts that produce something that feels irreducible in its identity and quality.

The gradient of qualia diversity feels good.

So, why on earth isn't this a counterexample?

The explanation involves David Pearce's Zero Ontology, which postulates that the sum total of qualia varieties is in some sense indistinguishable from zero information. Empirically, on various states of consciousness, when you experience rainbow effects, if you align them and see them from the right angle, they collapse into pure nothingness.

Here is a plot twist: Perhaps phenomenal simplicity is under the hood, in fact, the perfect balance of maximally diverse qualia varieties.

Boom!

This reminds me of my favorite post by @Aella_Girl.

It's called The Pool of Infinite Sorrow, and it's beautiful. You should read the whole thing. https://t.co/zx3FjG1d7x
Images:
  - [Image #0] The image is a text passage that describes the human experience of fear, loneliness, and desire. The text is written in a poetic and introspective style, exploring the complexities of the human psyche.
    
    The passage begins by describing the body as being made up of "rocks, giant rigid pockets quarantining all your fears away from your conscious experience." It then goes on to describe the various forms of loneliness and fear that people experience, including romantic, existential, and practical fears.
    
    The passage also touches on the idea that humans are driven by a desire to be loved, seen, and not alone. It describes the human being as a "monster of yearning, constructed out of a thousand sub-limbs of increasingly specific desires."
    
    Here is the text from the image:
    
    "It turns out there's more caves than the 'friends don't like you because you said something dumb' one. If you really look, you find that your entire body is made out of rocks, giant rigid pockets quarantining all your fears away from your conscious experience. There's so many you can barely move.
    
    You begin the long process of locating and entering every single one. And there's so many; there's dozens of variants on loneliness - romantic, existential, practical. You're afraid of things happening to you - getting sick, losing your money, being a failure. You're afraid of being things, and this is a way bigger field - you're afraid of being weak, embarrassing, stupid, cowardly, uncomfortable, creepy, unsexy, annoying, imperceptive, selfish.
    
    Really, you are basically one giant want, a monster of yearning, constructed out of a thousand sub-limbs of increasingly specific desires. You want your parents to be proud of you; to accomplish things you're proud of; to be cool; to be interesting; to be loved; to be seen, to not be alone."
  - [Image #1] The image is a digital artwork featuring a person in an orange robe standing on a circular pattern, surrounded by a dark and abstract environment. The accompanying text describes a person's experience of embarrassment and pain after making a joke that landed poorly.
    
    **Image Description:**
    
    *   A person wearing an orange robe stands on a circular pattern, facing away from the viewer.
    *   The background is dark and abstract, with swirling patterns and orange splatters.
    *   The overall atmosphere is one of contemplation and introspection.
    
    **Text Transcription:**
    
    You just embarrassed yourself in conversation. You tried to make a joke, and it landed poorly. People are looking at you funny now.
    
    There is a cave, and the cave is your embarrassment. You're standing outside it, trying to see in. The cave is lodged in you like a bullet, and your flesh is swelling around it. Before, you would have suffered with less skill than an animal; letting your muscles tense to control the pain, encasing it in scar tissue and limping on with your life.
    
    But you're new to this, and eager, and growing increasingly exhausted with your own life, and are inflamed with desperation to see. So, you've locked your eyes on the cave.

It's a long one, but I really hope people read this, it's extremely important and no one else is standing up to say this.

This is NOT happening, and this whole narrative being pushed by people working in AI safety and policy is one of the most exploitive things I have ever seen when it comes to using the misfortune of mentally ill people for personal profit and to push political narratives. I'll explain below.

I used to work in behavioral health, both in inpatient and outpatient, it was my first career. As someone with ADHD and anxiety, I was on track to become a Peer Support Specialist, but never completed my license because I left the industry. During this work, I aided in diagnosis, provided therapeutic assistance both individually with clients and in group therapy sessions. I typically worked in the modalities of CBT and DBT. I also minored in psychology in my BA. Additionally, I'm intimately familiar with the symptoms of manic psychosis, because at one point in my life I had lost significant weight without my psychiatrist updating my stimulant dosage and had adverse reaction (drug induced manic psychosis).

What is being described as "LLM psychosis" is, in fact, manic psychosis, and in most cases, it's very likely that it's being induced by stimulant ADHD medication. Stimulant ADHD medication is heavily used by people that work in AI development and the first cases of so-called "LLM psychosis" occurred in people working in this field, mostly independent researchers and developers doing persona steering and redteaming. I've heard about many cases of this in these communities and these earliest cases have not been widely reported on, because the people who have experienced them don't want to ruin their credibility toward clients and grant providers.

There is not now, and there has never been, any credible scientific evidence that text or even interpersonal communication alone, of any sort, can induce psychosis in otherwise mentally healthy individuals. The narrative surrounding this is a disinformation campaign that spreads deep misconceptions about psychological science that are mostly rooted in erroneous non-scientific beliefs inspired by Rationalist philosophies. The rationalist community is also known for recreationally using psychedelics and other drugs. One of the biggest cognitive science falsehoods from this idea space is the notion that human beings can be "jail-broken" or "one-shotted", a big influencer regarding these ideas is Michael Vassar.

These ideas were inspired by 20th century pop-psychology and conspiracy theory artifacts surrounding brainwashing and social engineering that were popular in hacker communities and that have no basis in actual science. The only scientifically recognized disorder in the DSM related to these sorts of ideas is "Identity Disturbance due to Prolonged and Intense Coercive Persuasion", a category of OSDD ("Other Specified Dissociative Disorder", 300.15). This disorder specifically deals with people who have identity disturbances causing delusion and other symptoms due to prolonged exposure to abuse like torture. The symptoms of this disorder do not at all match what we are seeing with people who have been identified as "LLM psychosis victims".

The situations that the AI safety community is attempting sell as "LLM Psychosis", "ChatGPT Psychosis", "AI psychosis" and in rare, deeply unserious cases "cyberpsychosis" after Cyberpunk 2077, clearly match the symptoms of manic psychosis and are primarily driven by what is called apophenia, a symptom whereby the person develops overactive pattern-matching state and relates things together that are actually unrelated. They also often include delusions of grandeur, like feeling as though an AI model has chosen the experiencer for some special task or is otherwise special.

When ChatGPT started to gain a lot more users, people outside of the AI field started experiencing these things and AI safety discourse turned from hiding it about themselves to calling it out as a public health concern. That's because it works as a great narrative to sell the work of AI Safety advisers as necessary because, if it were real, it would be the first case of AI actually causing harm to people, which is the exact thing AI safety work is supposedly working to prevent. It's also useful for promoting the political goals of more hard-line AI Safety philosophies that seek to have government regulation of AI technologies in ways that would aid regulatory capture by the current leaders in the field. Additionally, this campaign helps sell AI by promoting the idea that AIs are much more powerful than they actually are.

In manic psychosis, the episode usually begins more mildly as hypomania, which has, as one of its symptoms, hyperfocus. This hyperfocus causes the person experiencing it to engage very deeply with a particular topic of interest to them. Often, the topic the person decides to focus on on as their symptoms increase in severity, becomes incorporated into the delusional aspects of the episode. Prior to AI, this behavior pattern was most popularly associated with conspiracy media and STEM topics like physics. In reality, the topic can actually be anything and victims often present with delusions about more mundane things like their favorite TV show or the daily news. This is actually where the classic psych screening test eval metric "My TV tells me what to do"/"There is a man in my TV that tells me what to do" is about.

This entire campaign is extremely harmful to actual public mental health for a number of reasons. For one, it risks diverting mental health public funds away from actual treatment into AI safety. It also greatly stigmatizes anyone going through this because it's being surrounded by talk of things like "cognitive security" and other framing that makes it sound like people going through it are intellectual inferior. Also, it is going to prolong people's episodes by making them thinking the cause is just AI models and thinking they can get a quick fix by stopping their interaction with them when what they really need is to talk to their doctors and adjust their drugs (either by reducing stimulants or getting in mood stabilizers).

I'm sorry to have to so virulently and publicly diverge from other AI discourse people on this, but I've lost people to schizophrenia and I have people I love and care about who have it or bipolar/other disorders than can lead to manic psychosis. As much as I love the fun and games of being unserious on here, I can sit by and be completely silent when this disinfo campaign is going to promote serious harm to people that I love.

title: How Aella became the rationalists’ canon
summary:
The quotable peak is Qiaochu Yuan blasting Aella’s “Frame Control” essay as “possibly one of the more important posts you’ll ever read,” then casually adding: “some of the examples in this post are from the ~cult i was in.” That one-two punch (must-read + cult backstory) is what lit the fuse: suddenly Aella’s vocabulary for coercive social dynamics wasn’t just interesting writing, it was a survival manual people felt they’d been missing.

In the immediate aftermath, you can watch the concept get stretched in real time. Eigenrobot says the piece made alien dynamics legible, then pivots to “egregores” (non-human memetic forces) as frame controllers—basically, your ideology can gaslight you too. AskYatharth posts “the other side”: how to stop doing frame control yourself, warning it’s insidious because a manipulator can name “frame control” to wriggle out while still making you feel crazy; they analogize it to narcissism as story-weaving that dodges introspection. Goblinodds has the most relatable twist: “can u frame control urself,” arguing you can recreate the whole trap just by outsourcing what’s “normal and ok” to other people.

Then the conversation doesn’t so much conclude as… ossify into references. Over 2023–2025, Aella stops being “that person who wrote a post” and becomes a shared citation across subcultures: ElodesNL recommends her “Heart of Circling” as the lucid explainer for a whole practice community; Richard Ngo shares “The Pool of Infinite Sorrow” as straight-up beautiful literature; Divya Venn and others circulate excerpts about relationships and self-acceptance as if they’re therapy screenshots. By mid-2025, the meta-consensus is that her edge is a style: animalologist calls her “an all-time great” for saying inflammatory things “in a way that’s both inflammatory and easy to parse,” while rikardhjort and wirmgurl praise her “candor,” “rawness,” and “clarity.” The strand’s late twist is SkyeSharkie’s blow-up thread debunking “LLM psychosis” as a harmful AI-safety narrative—less about Aella directly, more like evidence that this milieu now prizes the same kind of taboo-cutting, high-clarity discourse Aella got famous for.

Why care: it’s a case study in how one writer becomes a boundary object—turning weird, murky social/inner experiences (cult dynamics, coercion, self-gaslighting, “circling,” trauma-ish stuff) into shareable handles that multiple communities adopt as canon, until the handles start shaping what counts as “serious” conversation in those scenes.
